handsOnLab.brief: You will audit the listening ports on a Windows machine, classify every listener as legitimate or suspicious, and write the workstation inbound rule set that a default-deny endpoint firewall would enforce. Listener inventory to policy — the concrete skill.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every listening port is classified with its owning process; the rule set covers all legitimate listeners with scoped allows and denies everything else.
handsOnLab.deliverable: listener-inventory.csv plus workstation-firewall-rules.md — the audit and the rule set.
steps: On a Windows test machine, run Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Select-Object LocalPort, OwningProcess | Sort-Object LocalPort -Unique to list listening TCP ports.
For each listening port, resolve the owning process: Get-Process -Id <PID> | Select-Object Name, Path — record process name and path.
Classify each listener: EXPECTED (system services, approved apps), REVIEW (unknown process listening — investigate), REMOVE (unneeded service — disable it).
Check UDP listeners too: Get-NetUDPEndpoint | Select-Object LocalPort, OwningProcess — classify the same way.
For each EXPECTED listener, write the firewall rule it needs: port, protocol, allowed remote scope (e.g., 'loopback only,' 'management subnet only,' 'local subnet'), and justification.
Write the default rules first: deny all inbound, deny workstation-to-workstation (SMB 445, RDP 3389, WinRM 5985/5986 between peers), then add your scoped exceptions above them.
Write the egress baseline: allow web (80/443) for approved browsers/apps, allow DNS to the company resolvers, deny-by-default egress for unknown processes.
Test one rule live: use New-NetFirewallRule to block outbound for a test process, verify with Test-NetConnection that the connection fails, then remove the rule.
Document the dynamic-ACL concept for two of your rules: under what condition does the port open (e.g., 'while the approved backup agent runs') and when does it close.
Write the troubleshooting runbook: app breaks after firewall change — identify the blocked flow (log), check the owning process, verify the destination, write the scoped exception.
Read the finished rule set as an attacker on the LAN: name which of your allowed rules you would abuse for lateral movement — then tighten the scope of the riskiest one.

mockTask.q: Panel question: 'Ransomware is spreading workstation to workstation over SMB. What does the endpoint firewall do about it?'

notes.body: Network Control is the endpoint firewall: the deny-by-default gate for packets, just as allowlisting is the gate for code. It manages dynamic access control lists on the machine itself — ports that open and close automatically based on policy and application need — and its two headline jobs are blocking lateral movement and blocking command-and-control callbacks. Understand first why the endpoint firewall is not redundant with the network firewall. The network firewall guards segments: it sees packets, applies rules per subnet, and stops at the perimeter. The endpoint firewall guards the machine: it sees the owning process behind every connection, applies policy per process identity, and follows the laptop to the café, the home office, and the customer site. That per-process visibility is the superpower: when the network firewall logs 'blocked outbound to evil.com,' you know a packet was stopped; when the endpoint firewall logs it, you know which process, launched by whom, from what parent, tried to call out — the exact context the M07 triage workflow needs. The baseline posture has four parts. Default-deny inbound: nothing may initiate connections to the machine unless policy explicitly permits it. Default-deny workstation-to-workstation: peers do not talk to peers — SMB, RDP, and WinRM between workstations are denied, which is the containment wall from the M01 assume-breach design. Scoped exceptions with justification: every allow names the ports, the remote scope, and the business reason. Default-deny egress for unknown processes: outbound connections are gated by process identity, so malware cannot simply phone home. Worked example: the café laptop. An employee works from a coffee shop on untrusted Wi-Fi. The network firewall is irrelevant — there is none. The endpoint firewall enforces the identical policy it enforces in the office: inbound denied, peer traffic denied, the browser allowed to 80/443, the unknown process's callback denied. The policy follows the machine because it lives on the machine. Common gotcha: 'we have a network firewall, so host firewall is redundant.' The network firewall never sees the laptop at the café, never knows which process opened the connection, and cannot enforce per-process identity. They are complementary layers, not substitutes. Second gotcha: managing endpoint firewall rules like network firewall rules — static, wide, forgotten. Endpoint rules should be dynamic and scoped: open when the approved application needs the port, closed when it does not, reviewed on the same cadence as the allowlist.  The endpoint firewall also feeds the EDR's network visibility: connection logs with process attribution are among the highest-value telemetry for threat hunting, because they show which process talked to where — the question every investigation asks first. Ensure the firewall logs are forwarded to the same store as the Detect alerts so the triage workflow sees them together: the blocked lateral attempt and the process tree in one view. A firewall whose logs stay local is a witness that never testifies.
notes.title: The endpoint firewall: packets get deny-by-default too

notes.body: Static firewall rules are standing invitations: a port opened 'temporarily' in 2021 is still open, still probed, still waiting. Dynamic ACLs fix this by tying the port's state to policy and need — the port opens when the approved application requires it and closes when it does not, automatically. The concept is easiest to grasp through the contrast. Static rule: 'allow inbound TCP 8080 from anywhere, forever' — written for a demo, forgotten, discovered by a scanner within the hour, exploited within the month. Dynamic rule: 'when the approved backup agent (signed, allowlisted) starts its receive window, open TCP 8443 from the backup server's IP only; close it when the window ends' — the port exists for minutes per day, from one source, for one purpose. An attacker scanning at any other time finds nothing. The 'automatically' matters operationally: nobody files a ticket to open and close the port, so nobody forgets to close it. Worked example: the patch-management agent. Once a week it needs inbound connections from the management server to receive tasks. Static approach: port 8530 open from the management subnet permanently — a standing target that any compromised machine on that subnet can probe. Dynamic approach: the ACL opens 8530 from the single management server IP during the agent's maintenance window and closes it after. The weekly exposure drops from 168 hours to 2, from a subnet to a single IP. Multiply that across every service and the machine's attack surface becomes a flickering target instead of a lit runway. The design discipline: every allow rule states its trigger (what opens it), its scope (from whom), and its lifetime (when it closes). Rules without lifetimes are static rules with better marketing — audit for them specifically. Common gotcha: dynamic ACLs for user applications that 'need' inbound. Workstations almost never legitimately need inbound connections — the application claiming to need one is usually misconfigured (it should poll outbound) or is peer-to-peer software that does not belong on the workstation. Challenge every inbound request on a workstation; the answer is usually 'redesign the app flow,' not 'open the port.' Second gotcha: confusing dynamic with permissive. Dynamic does not mean 'opens whenever asked' — it means 'opens when policy's conditions are met.' The conditions are the control.  Give every rule a lifecycle, not just a creation. The rule record states the owner, the justification, the review date, and the condition under which it is removed (project end, decommission, migration complete). Review the rule set on the same cadence as the allowlist — quarterly at minimum — and expire rules whose justification has lapsed. Firewall rules, like allowlist entries, rot: the 'temporary' vendor access from last year's migration is still open, and the scanner will find it before you remember it.
notes.title: Dynamic ACLs: ports that open and close themselves

notes.body: Lateral movement is how one compromised machine becomes an enterprise incident, and the endpoint firewall is where you strangle it. The attacker's playbook after landing is always the same: recon the local network, authenticate to neighbors with stolen credentials, and spread. Every step of that playbook needs network paths between workstations — and the default-deny endpoint posture removes them. The three protocols to know are SMB (TCP 445, file sharing and the classic ransomware-spread vector), RDP (TCP 3389, remote desktop — the attacker's interactive console), and WinRM (TCP 5985/5986, remote management — the administrator's tool turned against them). On a workstation, inbound connections on all three from peer workstations are denied by default. Not 'monitored.' Denied. The legitimate uses get scoped exceptions, not blanket allows: IT support reaches workstations through the approved remote-access tool (which has its own policy and logging), not through open RDP; management traffic comes from the management servers, not from peers. Worked example: the 9:04 AM ransomware spread from the M01 trace. The compromised workstation begins enumerating neighbors over SMB. Each connection attempt hits the neighbor's endpoint firewall: inbound 445 from a peer workstation — denied, logged. The ransomware tries RDP with a stolen credential — inbound 3389 from a peer — denied, logged. It tries WinRM — denied, logged. Three protocols, dozens of attempts, zero successes, and each denial emits a Detect alert with the source machine identified — so the SOC knows patient zero within minutes, from the firewall logs alone. The compromised machine is now an island: it can damage itself, but it cannot recruit. That is assume breach made concrete. Common gotcha: the 'server exception' creep. 'The workstation needs SMB inbound for the scanner' — no, the scanner needs an approved, scoped path, not peer SMB. Every workstation-to-workstation exception is a lateral-movement path you built on purpose; each needs a ticket, a justification, and a review date. Second gotcha: IPv6 and alternate protocols. Denying TCP 445 while leaving the same services reachable over alternate transports is a wall with a side door — the lateral-movement policy must cover the protocol family, verified by testing from a lab machine, not by reading the rule list.  Verify the lateral-movement policy across transports, not just the famous ports. Denying TCP 445 while the same file-sharing capability is reachable over an alternate transport is a wall with a side door. Your validation should attempt the lateral movement from a lab machine using the actual techniques — not just read the rule list — and confirm each path is denied and logged. The test matrix covers the protocol families your environment actually runs, including the ones the server team forgot to mention.
notes.title: Lateral-movement prevention: strangling the spread

notes.body: If lateral movement is the attacker's expansion, the command-and-control callback is their lifeline: the compromised machine must talk to the attacker's infrastructure to receive instructions, exfiltrate data, or download stage two. Network Control cuts the lifeline with egress filtering — outbound connections gated by process identity. The rule is simple: approved processes may reach approved destinations; unknown processes reach nothing. When the M01 ransomware tried to contact its server over HTTPS at 9:04:40, the egress policy evaluated the owning process: unknown binary, no rule — denied. The callback failed before the first byte, and the attempt became a Detect alert naming the process. Note what this does to the attacker's economics. Without egress filtering, any code that runs gets a free phone line home. With it, the attacker must hijack an approved process's legitimate connection — possible (browser injection, for example) but far harder and noisier than a direct callback. The destination side matters too: even approved processes should not reach arbitrary destinations. The browser may reach the web — that is its job — but the backup agent should reach only the backup infrastructure, the updater only the vendor's endpoints. This is the network equivalent of ringfencing: the allowed app gets the network scope its function needs, nothing more. Worked example: the updater compromise scenario. An attacker compromises a software vendor and trojans the update (the supply-chain nightmare). The trojaned updater is signed by the vendor, so it passes the allowlist. It tries to phone home to the attacker's server — but the updater's network fence permits only the vendor's update endpoints. Denied, logged, alerted. The supply-chain attack dies at the egress gate because the destination was never in the approved set. This is defense in depth paying off: the layer that failed (identity) is caught by the layer that constrains behavior (network scope). Common gotcha: 'allow all outbound HTTPS' as the egress policy. HTTPS to anywhere is a callback channel with encryption — the attacker's favorite. Egress policy must be per-process and per-destination-class, or it is not a policy. Second gotcha: DNS. Egress filtering on connections without DNS filtering leaves the DNS-tunneling path open — the complete design filters both, and the M07 triage workflow treats anomalous DNS as the signal it is.  Treat DNS as part of the egress policy, not as someone else's problem. Malware that cannot open a direct connection will try DNS tunneling — encoding data in DNS queries — which sails through a firewall that filters connections but not name resolution. The complete design points endpoints at company resolvers, logs and inspects DNS queries, and treats anomalous DNS (high entropy, unusual query rates, tunneling patterns) as the detection signal it is. The M07 triage workflow should include a DNS-history check for any host under investigation.
notes.title: Blocking C2: cutting the lifeline with egress filtering

notes.body: Servers and workstations need opposite firewall postures, and applying the wrong template is a classic junior mistake. Workstations consume: they browse, they run office apps, they talk to servers. They almost never need to accept inbound connections — so workstation policy is default-deny inbound, period, with rare scoped exceptions (the approved remote-support tool, the management agent's window). Servers serve: the web server must accept inbound 80/443, the file server must accept SMB from its clients, the domain controller must accept authentication traffic. Server policy is therefore scoped-allow inbound per service: each listening service gets a rule naming the ports, the permitted sources, and nothing else. The discipline is identical — least privilege — but the shape inverts: workstations deny nearly everything inbound, servers allow precisely what they serve. Worked example: the mis-templated web server. A new web server accidentally receives the workstation firewall template: inbound 80/443 denied, and the site is down. The fix is not 'open everything' — it is the server template: allow TCP 80/443 inbound from the load balancer and the monitoring hosts, allow admin ports (RDP/SSH/WinRM) from the jump host only, deny everything else, and deny server-to-workstation initiation except the management paths. Conversely, the workstation that someone 'fixed' by applying the server template now accepts inbound SMB from the subnet — a lateral-movement gift. The rule: the template follows the role, and role changes trigger policy review. The management-plane design deserves its own attention: servers need administration, and administration needs paths. The correct pattern is the jump host (or privileged access workstation): admin protocols are permitted only from the hardened jump host to the servers, never from workstations to servers directly, and never between servers except the specific service traffic. This turns the admin path into a chokepoint you can monitor, log, and protect — instead of a mesh of standing admin access. Common gotcha: 'the server needs internet access' as a blanket statement. Servers need specific destinations (update servers, vendor endpoints, monitoring) — each named, each scoped. A server with unrestricted outbound is a C2 launchpad waiting for a compromise. Second gotcha: forgetting the server's own workstation-like behaviors. Servers browse the web for 'quick downloads' — they should not; software comes through the deployment pipeline. The server egress policy should be as tight as its inbound.  Harden the jump host like the crown jewel it is: no internet browsing, no email, allowlisted applications only, every session logged, and access requiring phishing-resistant authentication. A compromised jump host inherits its administrative reach — the chokepoint becomes the prize. Review who holds jump-host access quarterly, because the list grows silently and every name on it is a path to every server. The jump host is the one machine where 'inconvenient security' is the entire point.
notes.title: Server vs workstation: opposite postures, same discipline

notes.body: Firewall policy is the number-one suspect when 'the app worked yesterday,' so the troubleshooting discipline must be structured — random rule-toggling creates holes. The triage order is fixed. Step one: identify the blocked flow. Pull the firewall log for the timeframe: source, destination, port, protocol, direction, and — the endpoint firewall's gift — the owning process. Most 'mystery outages' end here: the log names the exact denied connection. Step two: check the owning process against policy. Is this process approved? Is it the legitimate application or something wearing its name? Verify identity (hash, certificate, path) before touching any rule — opening a port for malware because 'the app needed it' is the classic self-inflicted breach. Step three: verify the destination's legitimacy. Is this the vendor's real update endpoint or a lookalike? Check DNS, check the vendor's published endpoints, be suspicious of anything newly registered. Step four: write the scoped exception. The exception names the process, the ports, the destination scope, and the justification — and it goes above the deny rules, documented, with a review date. Never 'allow all outbound for the app to see if that fixes it' — that is not troubleshooting, it is surrender. Worked example: Monday 9 AM, the accounting package cannot reach its cloud service after a weekend policy push. Triage: the firewall log shows denied outbound TCP 443 from AcctApp.exe to 203.0.113.45. Process check: AcctApp.exe is allowlisted, signed by the vendor, parent chain clean. Destination check: 203.0.113.45 is in the vendor's published endpoint list (verified via the vendor's docs, not the user's word). Verdict: the weekend policy tightened egress without the vendor's endpoint range. Fix: scoped exception — AcctApp.exe may reach the vendor's published endpoint range on 443, documented with the ticket, review in 90 days. Total downtime: 20 minutes, because the triage order went straight to the evidence. Common gotcha: the 'temporary allow-any' that becomes permanent. Every troubleshooter is tempted; the discipline is writing the scoped rule even under pressure, because the emergency you fix today with a hole becomes the incident you investigate next quarter. Second gotcha: troubleshooting the firewall when the problem is DNS, the proxy, or the application itself. The firewall log is step one precisely because it tells you in seconds whether the firewall is even involved — if there is no denied flow, look elsewhere.  Record every exception in the change system with the same five fields as the allowlist: requester, justification, scope, expiry, approver. The firewall exception register is audited alongside the others, and 'temporary vendor access' without an expiry is the rule most likely to be found open two years later. When the auditor asks why port X is open to subnet Y, the register should answer in one lookup — that is the difference between a managed firewall and a collection of rules.
notes.title: When the firewall breaks the app: structured triage

summary: Packets get deny-by-default too. This module covers the endpoint firewall: dynamic ACLs that open and close ports automatically, lateral-movement prevention that contains a compromise to one machine, egress filtering that starves C2 callbacks, the inverted postures of servers vs workstations, and structured triage when the firewall breaks a legitimate app.
